facts.text: The olive-backed oriole is a very common medium-sized bird native to northern and eastern Australia and south-central New Guinea.
facts.quote: The olive-backed oriole (Oriolus sagittatus), or white-bellied oriole, is a very common medium-sized passerine bird native to northern and eastern Australia and south-central New Guinea.

facts.text: It is the most wide-ranging of the Australasian orioles and is noisy and conspicuous.
facts.quote: The most wide-ranging of the Australasian orioles, it is noisy and conspicuous.

facts.text: The olive-backed oriole is not bright in colour, with an olive back marked by small dark streaks.
facts.quote: Not bright in colour, it is olive-backed with small dark streaks, with a light chest having black streaks.

facts.text: Females have cinnamon-edged wings, and both sexes have reddish bills and eyes.
facts.quote: Females have cinnamon-edged wings and both sexes have reddish bills and eyes.

facts.text: Unlike the green oriole, it prefers more open woodland environments and tolerates drier climates, though not the desert.
facts.quote: the olive-backed oriole is more versatile, preferring more open woodland environments, and tolerating drier climates (but not desert).

facts.text: Its range stretches from the very north of Western Australia across the east and south coasts to Victoria and the corner of South Australia.
facts.quote: Their range is from the very north of Western Australia across the east and south coasts to Victoria and the corner of South Australia.

facts.text: It is common to very common in the north but less frequently seen in the south, reaching as far as south-eastern South Australia.
facts.quote: While common to very common in the north, olive-backed orioles are less frequently seen in the south, but nevertheless reach as far as south-eastern South Australia.

facts.text: Most olive-backed orioles breed during the tropical wet season, but some migrate south to breed in the southern summer.
facts.quote: Most birds breed during the tropical wet season, but some migrate south to breed in the southern summer.

facts.text: The species was originally described in the genus Coracias by the English ornithologist John Latham in 1801.
facts.quote: The olive-backed oriole was originally described in the genus Coracias by the English ornithologist John Latham in 1801.
